Great meeting with VP @JDVance on Friday to discuss American AI leadership, cybersecurity, and modernizing our nation’s software infrastructure.

New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. 

We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters.

- Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents.

- GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents.

- Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination.

- The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance.

- Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence.

We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling.

tweets.text:
This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.
2026 is just waking up each day to the magnitude of news that could only have happened once per decade before 2026.

tweets.text:
不懂政治的金融家，可能很难在华尔街长久地赚钱。

黄仁勋 @JensenHuang 复职前，木头姐 @CathieDWood 抛售了超 1 亿美元的英伟达股票。

7 月 28 日至 11 月 9 日，木头姐旗下 ARK ETF 在 9 个交易日累计加仓约 132.7 万股英伟达，加权参考均价为 210.09 美元，估算买入金额达 2.79 亿美元。

即便在黄仁勋遭遇舆论风波后，木头姐仍选择逆势抄底，11 月 5 日至 9 日累计买入约 6211 万美元。

然而，随着黄仁勋辞任 CEO，木头姐的交易方向发生逆转：

· 11 月 16 日，减持约 8480 万美元；
· 11 月 19 日，减持约 488 万美元；
· 11 月 20 日，减持约 1704 万美元。

三次累计减持 71.23 万股，估算金额达 1.07 亿美元，加权卖出参考价为 149.83 美元。

仅一个交易日后，黄仁勋宣布复职，英伟达单日暴涨 31.5%，收于 165.05 美元。若上述减持股份全部保留至当日收盘，其市值将较估算卖出金额高出约 1084 万美元。

从 210 美元加仓，到 150 美元减仓，木头姐看对了 AI 的产业趋势，却没能踩准这场政治博弈的节奏。

当英伟达这样的公司已经成为大国科技竞争的核心筹码，投资就不再只是一道财务分析题。

在这个时代，政治本身就是基本面的一部分。

注：交易金额及加权参考价格均按交易日收盘价估算，非实际成交数据。

黄仁勋回来了，《纽约时报》却似乎还没走出这场风波。

据 HyperspaceAI 创始人 Varun Mathur 统计，10 月 29 日至 11 月 14 日，《纽约时报》@nytchinese 共发布 88 条与黄仁勋婚外情及离职事件相关的内容，平均每天超过 5 条，并被 34 家媒体的 370 篇文章引用。

报道范围也在不断扩大，从个人私生活延伸至中国间谍、芯片走私、职场霸凌，甚至连黄仁勋标志性的皮夹克都成了批评对象。

黄仁勋辞职时，《纽约时报》将其视为美国的胜利；黄仁勋复职后，又批评特朗普纵容亿万富翁逃避追责，并继续公开征集英伟达相关新闻线索。

这场风波最值得关注的，或许是美国科技产业、政治权力与媒体话语权之间的博弈。

英伟达掌握着全球 AI 算力产业的核心资源，黄仁勋的对华立场、芯片出口主张以及与特朗普政府的关系，都让他早已不只是一家上市公司的 CEO。

88 条内容、370 篇引用，并不足以证明存在一场有组织的政治行动，但如此密集的报道及其议题演变，值得研究。

当媒体从追问事实走向预设立场，新闻监督与政治叙事之间的边界又在哪里？

黄仁勋一个人回归，全球科技股集体狂欢。

昨夜英伟达暴涨 31.48%，市值一夜增加 9520 亿美元，逼近 4 万亿美元。纳斯达克 100 成份股市值合计增加超 2 万亿美元，费城半导体指数大涨约 14%。

这场狂欢今早蔓延至亚洲市场：韩国 KOSPI 指数涨 6%，三星电子涨 9%，SK 海力士涨 10.5%；中国台湾加权指数涨 9.06%，台积电开盘即涨停；港股智谱、MiniMax 涨超 14%，A 股半导体、CPO、PCB 等板块集体上攻。

与此同时，马斯克 @elonmusk 谈及过去几周对黄仁勋 @JensenHuang 的力挺：「顺境时人人都是你的朋友，但逆境时支持你的人才是你真正的朋友。酒肉朋友一文不值。」

有意思的是，马斯克原文使用了「when the chips are up / down」，既指人生的顺境与逆境，也暗指芯片。

一场人事风波，让全球资本市场重新认识了黄仁勋的分量。

tweets.text: us spot bitcoin etfs lost $569.7m net on november 23, their fifth negative day in a row. blackrock's ibit made up $509.3m, or 89.4%, of it. november withdrawals now total $4.71b. that is more than june 2026's $4.51b, the worst full month in data since january 2024. so fund demand for btc is shrinking at a record monthly pace. ibit can pay redemptions in btc, so how much btc was sold on the market is not clear.

artist qubibi released sun on verse, an onchain art platform, on november 23. it is 100 ethereum nfts that use a phone's motion sensor to show a sun overhead, at $180 each. by the end of that day, 33 were minted. two other verse releases open on november 24 at $275. verse mints after purchase, so mint data does not show buyer numbers or purchase dates. it also cannot show if this is new demand or collector money moved from those other drops.

on november 23, cftc staff said regulated us derivatives venues and clearinghouses may count btc, eth and qualifying payment stablecoins toward the funds that must cover 12 months of operating costs. stablecoins take a 2% minimum haircut, and btc and eth take 20%. so $1m in stablecoins counts as $980k, against $800k in btc or eth. a separate six-month liquidity test still excludes all crypto, so how much cash firms can free depends on their credit lines. this is staff guidance, not a new rule.

tweets.text:
25万页是玩笑？Anthropic数学家发布证明后，把手搓12年的同行逼到提前公开未完成手稿

11月23日晚，Anthropic研究员Levent Alpöge发帖澄清，此前传得沸沸扬扬的“Claude证明黎曼猜想长达25万页”，只是他开的一个玩笑。

原帖大意是，自己觉得“大数字”特别好笑，故意把Lean代码写到极长，没想到全网都当真了。同时他承认，公开的Lean代码虽然能编译通过，但内部很乱，“全是垃圾”，外界批评完全合理。

不过关键的是他在评论区回复：强调证明本身没问题，几天前已经通过核验。

但玩笑已经造成后果

就在Alpöge宣布“与Claude证明黎曼猜想”的当天，美国数学学会主席Ravi Vakil紧急公开了斯坦福博士Alessandro Masullo的940页纯人手稿。

公开后几小时，就有人用AI找出问题，Masullo本人也承认手稿远未达到可提交状态。

在手稿前言里，他写下了这句话：

“我们还在这里。我们依然充满生命力。我们哪儿也不会去。”

这句话原本是写给那些被AI浪潮冲击得心灰意冷的数学家看的，结果却成了他自己提前被迫公开未完成工作后的注脚。

不过AI在速度和可验证性上的优势已经很明显——Lean形式化可以在短时间内完成大规模交叉检查，而人手稿再长也容易被快速定位问题。

目前数学界更关心的是：虽然Levent的黎曼猜想形式化验证通过了，可人类还是读不懂它为什么成立。

tweets.text:
The term AI agents sounds cringe

Which makes sense because it's primarily used by people in polycules keeping their MacBook lids open

In reality it's quite simple

If you were to hire someone to work for you, and you gave them a task with no prior guidance or training, you wouldn't be too surprised if they produced shit

AI models are the same

To get useful work out, you need to put effort in to give models the appropriate context, tools, and instructions

A common complaint from people is "I don't even know what I would ask it/what I would use it for."

You don't need to know the answer beforehand. If you give the model enough information, it will be able to propose pretty intelligent things itself.

The simplest way to kick this off would be to create a folder on your desktop (literally an empty folder) and then open up the Claude desktop app or whatever you use and point it at that folder

The reason you're pointing the model at a folder is that it can read, write, code, and remember shit instead of just being a fancy Google search that forgets everything

If you want bonus points you can go into Settings > Connectors/Plugins and give it read access to places where you do your work or hobbies e.g. your email, calendar, Google Drive etc.

Then you can fire off something as simple as:

I'm setting up this folder because I want to do cool shit with LLMs. I'm a total noob. If I've connected anything like my email or calendar, have a look through them first (read-only, don't touch or send anything). Then grill me a question or two at a time about my work, goals, hobbies, and whatever is currently wasting my time or cool stuff I want to do. Once you develop a decent understanding of me and my goals etc., write it all down in a file in this folder so you remember it next time. Then tell me 5 genuinely useful things you could actually do for me (skip the boring 'summarise my emails' slop) and we'll start on the best one.

That's it. You've just used an AI agent - congrats

You are just weeks away from vibe coding a Bloomberg terminal and 3D printing a fleshlight

推荐阅读《当你的客户不再是人类：a16z 万次实测揭秘 AI Agent 的消费偏好，企业如何赢得算法订单？》

https://t.co/mPGML0JAej

如果买你东西的不再是人类，而是冷冰冰的 AI，传统商业的营销套路可能彻底作废了。

a16z 最近联合机构完成了 1.1 万次 AI Agent 模拟下单测试。结果发现，机器花起钱来，根本不吃人类那一套：

平时宽泛的需求，便宜的竞品凭借性价比通吃；但只要需求稍微细化（比如吹风机限定“细软发质”），大牌的胜率立刻从个位数飙到 88%。通用拼低价，垂直才能吃溢价。

华丽的网店装修对机器毫无意义。官网再精美，如果防着机器、不给自动化留门，Agent 几秒钟就会转头把单子下给不知名的小竞品。算法眼里没有品牌光环，只有机器能不能直接读取。

算盘打得比人还精，但折扣过大直接被当成诈骗。降价低于 10% 机器根本没反应，但折扣一旦超过 50%，机器反而会触发风控警觉，当成假货全线回避。大部分情况下机器宁愿多花钱买官方正品。

结账环节更是生硬。支持免登录游客直接买的，跑通率 81%；只要中途弹出强制注册登录，机器 100% 当场放弃，扭头就转投竞品。

当消费者从人类变成算法，情感包装彻底失效。未来谁能让机器一秒读懂、顺畅结算，谁才能拿到算法的购买权。

No. Here’s what really happened.

Jensen started Nvidia in 1993, before the modern era of founder control and dual-class stock began with Google and Facebook.

Because he went public in the 1990s, he inherited all the 20th century overhead of endless public company paperwork, rather than staying private for as long as possible as is also now typical.

This is why Jensen had much less control than a modern founder/CEO. Like Jack Dorsey at Twitter, he got gradually boxed into a corner by the fact that he couldn’t raise huge amounts of capital outside his company to clear the board of cruft.

You see, as CEO, you report to the board. And you can’t do outside activities without their approval. So actions that would remove a board member that doesn’t want to step down are hard to take. Unless the CEO is also part of a shareholder majority, or has dual class / founder control, which Jensen didn’t in this case, as explained above…he can’t pick the board.

Like Bezos, though, Jensen is a workhorse and somehow made it all work despite that. Moreover, because Nvidia is a hardware company, and had a relatively low market cap until the AI boom, it didn’t attract notice from envious wokes until the last few years. 

Wokes don’t know or care about GPUs, but they do care about market caps, and the rise of AI, and especially open source AI, all of which is a threat to their power. Along with useful idiot “nationalists”, they began plotting to steal control of Jensen’s multi-trillion-dollar company from him.

In this plot, they were aided by a second angle of vulnerability. Jensen didn’t just have old board members he couldn’t remove. Due to DEI policies, he was also forced to bring new board members on, from demographics favored by the far left (eg, not veterans).

Conformist board members like this act like sleeper cells. They are often useless or inactive in peacetime scenarios. Then they activate in response to press or state pressure. In this case, they then got beaten back just as quickly by the reversal of the state’s position.

Anyway, Dorsey needed Elon to come in with his enormous new resources to sweep the board clean. Today, it’s quite possible that Jensen, as the survivor of this character assassination, will similarly figure out a way to fire this incompetent board and assert proper founder control — as is a best practice in the modern era.

Founders produce higher returns than non-founders. This is an empirical fact.

So: business school curricula should be changed, and good governance should be redefined as founder control and dual-class stock. Shareholders are still protected by easy liquidation and their ability to fund new entrants. After all, you don’t invest in a company based on who’s on the board. That’s largely ceremonial.

The key difference from the 20th century is that it was prohibitively difficult in 1950 to found a manufacturing company, because assembly lines cost so much, the communists controlled much of the world, and even America had 90% marginal tax rates. It was the century of centralization, the individual powerless before the institution.

Today it is no longer prohibitively difficult to found a tech company, because software costs so little, much of the world has turned to free markets, and capital flows at the speed of the Internet. This is the century of decentralization, at least in the West, with the institution falling to the individual.

For example: Anthropic was started just a few years ago and is beating even Google at its own game. If we get many open weights models, their moat will also in turn erode.

So: all 20th century corporate governance was based on the idea that “the company is hard to replace, but its CEO isn’t.” The Harvard MBA is premised on the professional manager. It was expensive to start a new company with all the assembly lines, so make sure it doesn’t fail by making every employee replaceable. Managers were abundant so capital became the scarce asset.

By contrast, the entire 21st century model is based on the idea that “A tech founder is hard to replace, but the company isn’t.” The YCombinator model is premised on the startup founder. It is inexpensive to start a new company with a few lines of code, so make sure it doesn’t fail by having an irreplaceable team. Capital is abundant so founders become the scarce asset.
